title: Lake Braies, Fanes‑Sennes‑Braies Nature Park, Dolomites, Italy
caption: Info
subtitle: Lake Braies, Fanes‑Sennes‑Braies Nature Park, Dolomites, Italy
description: Lake Braies sits almost 1,500 metres above sea level in the Dolomites of South Tyrol, northern Italy. Surrounded by forest and the dramatic peaks of the Fanes-Sennes-Braies Nature Park, the lake is known for its striking green and blue waters. A 3.5-kilometre trail circles the shore, while traditional wooden rowing boats offer another way to take in the scenery. The lake is also a starting point for several mountain walks, including the Dolomites' famous Alta Via 1.

title: Black Forest, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
caption: Info
subtitle: Black Forest, Baden-Württemberg, Germany
description: Today we're enjoying the misty views sweeping across the Black Forest, which stretches for around 160 kilometres across south-west Germany, bringing together wooded hills, deep valleys, lakes and charming towns. Its highest point, Feldberg, rises to 1,493 metres, while the Black Forest is also the starting point for the Danube and Neckar rivers. There's plenty of history and tradition here too. Forestry has long played an important role in the region, while its centuries-old clockmaking heritage helped make the distinctive cuckoo clock famous far beyond Germany.

title: Polar bear and cubs by Hudson Bay, Manitoba, Canada
caption: Info
subtitle: Polar bear and cubs by Hudson Bay, Manitoba, Canada
description:
These polar bears are gathering along the shores of Hudson Bay in Manitoba, Canada, waiting for sea ice to form so they can head back out to hunt seals. Polar bears are powerful swimmers, expert hunters and remarkably adapted to life in one of Earth's harshest environments. Yet shrinking sea ice means many spend longer on land, making it harder to find food and raising the risk of encounters with people.
The image captures a heartwarming scene: a mother and her cubs near Hudson Bay, where generations of bears have gathered seasonally. These iconic animals remind us not only of the Arctic's wild beauty, but also of the importance of protecting the frozen habitat they depend on.

title: Taquaras Beach, Balneário Camboriú, Brazil
caption: Info
subtitle: Taquaras Beach, Balneário Camboriú, Brazil
description: On Brazil's southern coast, Taquaras Beach offers a quieter escape in Balneário Camboriú, Santa Catarina. Clear blue-green waters meet a broad stretch of golden sand, backed by lush vegetation and rolling green hills. Away from the livelier atmosphere of the city centre, the beach is known for its peaceful surroundings and natural beauty. With its inviting shoreline, rich greenery and unspoilt feel, Taquaras showcases a calmer side of this popular Brazilian coastal destination.

title: People rowing among colourful bald cypress, Xuancheng, Anhui, China
caption: Info
subtitle: Bald cypress, Xuancheng, Anhui, China
description:
People paddle through a glowing maze of bald cypress in Xuancheng, Anhui, where autumn transforms flooded woodlands into a tapestry of amber, copper and deep rust. Known scientifically as 'Taxodium distichum', bald cypress is unusual among conifers because it sheds its soft, feathery needles each fall, turning reddish-brown before they drop.
Some specimens are exceptionally long-lived, with historical records reporting trees more than 1,000 years old. As rowers glide across the still water, they weave through a landscape that reflects the tree's natural affinity for wetlands. The scene is especially striking in late autumn, when the foliage shifts from green to fiery shades that shimmer across the water, turning the forest into a living painting.

title: Wooden stile at a stone wall, Black Crag, Lake District, England
caption: Info
subtitle: Black Crag, Lake District, England
description:
A simple wooden stile leads into one of England's most celebrated landscapes. The Lake District, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is a patchwork of shimmering lakes, rugged fells and centuries-old stone walls, all shaped by both nature and farming traditions.
This path leads towards Black Fell, whose rocky summit is known as Black Crag. At 323 metres, it may not be the tallest fell in the region, but its views are remarkable. From the top, hikers can look across Windermere, Coniston Water and the dramatic Langdale Pikes.
The route to Black Crag winds around Tarn Hows, one of the Lake District's most picturesque spots, before climbing steadily toward the summit. For those approaching via Tom Gill, the journey also passes through woodland alongside the tumbling waterfalls. Whether you come for a leisurely walk or a hilltop panorama, this corner of Cumbria packs an outsized sense of adventure into every step.

title: Bamboo forest, Pīpīwai Trail, Haleakalā National Park, Maui, Hawaii, USA
caption: Info
subtitle: Pīpīwai Trail, Haleakalā National Park, Maui, Hawaii
description:
A volcano, a rainforest and a bamboo grove? Haleakalā National Park on Maui has all three. Spanning Maui from its 3,055-metre summit to the coast, the park protects landscapes that change dramatically with elevation, rainfall and temperature. It was established in 1916 as part of Hawaii National Park and became its own national park in 1961. The name Haleakalā translates to 'House of the Sun', reflecting the Hawaiian mo'olelo of Māui capturing the sun to lengthen the day.
The park is home to more than 850 plant species, including the Haleakalā silversword, a plant found naturally only on the mountain, as well as native birds such as the nēnē and 'ua'u. In the Kīpahulu District, the Pīpīwai Trail heads through a wet forest to its famous bamboo grove. About a kilometre into the hike, the bamboo creates a canopy overhead, with its stalks making distinctive sounds when the wind moves through them.

title: A bison in the grasslands of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, North Dakota, USA
caption: Info
description: Bison are among the largest land mammals in the world, capable of weighing up to 900 kilograms and reaching speeds of 65 kilometres per hour despite their massive size. Despite often being called a buffalo, the American bison is not one of the true buffaloes, which are native to Africa and Asia. Its scientific name, Bison bison, leaves little room for confusion.
